draft.title: Trade agreements and tariffs
card: Tariff
A tariff is a tax on imports. The importer pays it when the goods enter the country, so imported goods usually cost more.
Protection
A tariff can protect local producers. Imports become dearer, so local goods can compete better and local firms may sell more.
Cost
Tariffs also raise prices for buyers. Shoppers may pay more for imports, and for local goods too, when local firms face less competition.
Free trade agreement
A free trade agreement is a deal between countries to cut or remove tariffs on each other's goods. The aim is to increase trade between them.
draft.remember: Tariffs shield local producers but raise prices. Free trade agreements cut tariffs to increase trade.

a.q: A government adds a tariff to imported bicycles. What is the most likely effect on local bicycle makers?
opts: They are protected, because imports cost more
They lose sales, because local bikes cost more
They are unaffected, because buyers pay the tariff
They face more competition, because imports cost less
a.why: A tariff makes imported bikes dearer, so local makers can compete better. The tempting option that local makers lose sales has it backwards: the tariff is placed on imports, not on local bikes.
a.clue: Who pays the tax: imports or local goods?

b.q: Country A and Country B sign a free trade agreement. Country A's farmers used to pay a tariff to sell cheese in B. What is the most likely result?
opts: A's cheese becomes cheaper in B, so trade can rise
A's cheese becomes dearer in B, so trade can fall
B's local cheesemakers gain protection from A's cheese
B's government collects a bigger tariff on A's cheese
b.why: The agreement cuts tariffs, so A's cheese costs less in B and more may be sold. The tempting option about protection describes what a tariff does, but the agreement removes that tariff, so B's cheesemakers lose it.
b.clue: What does a free trade agreement do to tariffs?

a.best: They are protected, because imports cost more

b.best: A's cheese becomes cheaper in B, so trade can rise

problems.detail: The stem says Country A's farmers 'used to pay a tariff to sell cheese in B'. The card says the importer pays the tariff when goods enter the country, so here B's importers would pay it, not A's exporting farmers. The stem contradicts the card and could confuse students about who pays a tariff.
